Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: 43-year-old male with well-controlled T2DM and mild hypertension presents with acute upper-respiratory symptoms; exam limited to mild pharyngeal erythema, no lower-respiratory signs.  
Working diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold).  
Differential diagnoses:  
• Influenza/influenza-like illness – moderate likelihood given systemic symptoms but mild course and afebrile.  
• ACE-inhibitor–induced cough – low–moderate likelihood; dry cough but abrupt onset and concurrent viral symptoms argue against.  
Management priorities: Provide symptomatic relief, ensure ongoing monitoring, reinforce red-flag advice, and continue chronic disease medications.

Management Plan

- Symptomatic care: Night Nurse/Day Nurse preparations permissible with current medications.  
- Continue regular medications (metformin, lisinopril).  
- Safety-net advice: Seek review if shortness of breath, wheeze, or if symptoms persist >3 weeks or worsen.  
- No antibiotics or further investigations indicated today.  
- Follow-up: PRN telehealth review if red-flags develop.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits): Not recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral: Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support): Not recorded.

- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test): Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Viral upper respiratory tract infection – High likelihood: acute onset, rhinorrhea, dry cough, pharyngeal erythema, systemic aches; self-limited.  
2. Influenza/influenza-like illness – Moderate likelihood: cough plus chills, myalgias, headache; absence of high fever lowers probability.  
3. ACE-inhibitor (lisinopril)–induced cough – Low–Moderate likelihood: dry cough and ACE-I use, but concurrent viral features and short duration make this less likely.
